current_activity: Arrives from England in Normandy and joins the 21st Army Group at Falaise, about 4,000 strong
notes: Event date: 30 August 1944 (Wikipedia). Event definition: After training in the United Kingdom until the summer of 1944 the brigade group, some 4,000 troops, moves to Normandy and joins the 21st Army Group at Falaise. Event support: one source family (Wikipedia). Wikipedia, 1st Czechoslovak Independent Armoured Brigade, section Siege of Dunkirk: "with some 4,000 troops under command, it moved to Normandy, joining 21st Army Group at Falaise on 30 August". Location: Falaise, Calvados with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the town; the brigade assembled in the area, so precision 10 km. Location support: Wikipedia names Falaise as the place where it joined the army group. Commander: Major-General A. Liska (Alois Liška) commands the brigade group (Stacey, p. 368; Wikipedia).

source_locator: R668: p. 368; R675: section Siege; R037: section Siege of Dunkirk
current_activity: Takes over the containment of Dunkirk from the 154th Brigade, under First Canadian Army
notes: Event date: 9 October 1944 (Stacey, p. 368; Wikipedia, Siege of Dunkirk; the brigade article has it advancing to Dunkirk on 6 October). Event definition: The brigade group relieves the 154th (Highland) Infantry Brigade on the eastern side of the Dunkirk perimeter and takes over the containment of the fortress, with a French infantry battalion and French Forces of the Interior under it; it comes under First Canadian Army, which has had the containing force directly under its headquarters since 26-27 September. Event support: two source families (Stacey, the Canadian official history and Wikipedia). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 368: "on 9 October the 154th Brigade handed over the task at Dunkirk to the 1st Czechoslovak Independent Armoured Brigade Group, commanded by Major-General A. Liska"; Wikipedia, Siege of Dunkirk (1944-1945), section Siege: "On 9 October, the 1st Czechoslovak Armoured Brigade took over the siege"; Wikipedia, 1st Czechoslovak Independent Armoured Brigade, section Siege of Dunkirk: "relieved the 154 (Highland) Infantry Brigade on the eastern side of fortress Dunkirk". Location: Dunkirk, Nord with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the town; the brigade held the containing line round the fortress, mainly on the eastern side, so precision 10 km. Location support: Stacey and both Wikipedia articles name Dunkirk; the brigade article places it on the eastern side. Location caveat: the Wikipedia brigade article says the brigade advanced to Dunkirk on 6 October; the handover date of 9 October (Stacey; Wikipedia, Siege of Dunkirk) is used. Commander: Major-General A. Liska (Alois Liška) commands the brigade group (Stacey, p. 368; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Containment of Dunkirk: limited attack on Czechoslovak Independence Day takes over 300 prisoners
notes: Event date: 28 October 1944 (Stacey, p. 368; Wikipedia, Siege of Dunkirk). Event definition: On Czechoslovak Independence Day the brigade makes a limited attack into the Dunkirk perimeter which takes over 300 prisoners. Event support: two source families (Stacey, the Canadian official history and Wikipedia). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 368: "they celebrated their country's Independence Day, 28 October, with a limited attack which netted over 300 prisoners"; Wikipedia, Siege of Dunkirk (1944-1945), section Siege: "an attack on 28 October (Czechoslovak independence day) took 300 prisoners". Location: Dunkirk, Nord with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the town; the sector of the attack is not named in the sources read (the brigade raided mainly into the eastern suburbs), so precision 10 km. Location support: both families place the attack at Dunkirk without naming the sector. Commander: Major-General A. Liska (Alois Liška) commands the brigade group (Stacey, p. 368; Wikipedia). Opponents: the German garrison of Dunkirk.

current_activity: Containment of Dunkirk: passes from First Canadian Army to direct command of the 21st Army Group
notes: Event date: 27 November 1944 (Stacey, p. 368; Wikipedia gives only November). Event definition: The brigade group, still containing Dunkirk, leaves First Canadian Army and comes under direct command of the 21st Army Group. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 368: "remained under First Canadian Army until 27 November, when they passed"; "under direct command of the 21st Army Group". Location: Dunkirk, Nord with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the town; the brigade held the containing line round it, so precision 10 km. Location support: Stacey p. 368 keeps the brigade at Dunkirk until the end of the campaign. Relationship: the attachment to First Canadian Army ends on this day and both relations include it, so the parent of the row is First Canadian Army (the operational parent on the day of the change); from 28 November the brigade is under the 21st Army Group only Commander: Major-General A. Liska (Alois Liška) commands the brigade group (Stacey, p. 368; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Still investing Dunkirk at the end of the campaign; the garrison surrenders to Liska on 9 May
notes: Event date: 8 May 1945, representative date (Stacey, p. 368: until the end of the campaign; Ellis, vol. II, p. 343, early May; Wikipedia: surrender on 9 May). Event definition: The brigade group, under direct command of the 21st Army Group, is still investing the fortress of Dunkirk at the end of the campaign (a token force has left to join the US Third Army); the garrison surrenders to General Liska on 9 May, after the end of the dataset. Event support: three source families (Stacey, the Canadian official history, Ellis, the British official history and Wikipedia). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 368: "They stayed at Dunkirk until the end of the campaign"; Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 343: "Twenty-First Army Group's Czech Armoured Brigade (which was then still investing the German 'fortress' of Dunkirk)"; Wikipedia, Siege of Dunkirk (1944-1945), section Siege: "The garrison surrendered unconditionally to Liška on 9 May 1945". Location: Dunkirk, Nord with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the town; the brigade held the containing line round it, so precision 10 km. Location support: all three families keep the brigade at Dunkirk to the end of the war. Commander: Major-General A. Liska (Alois Liška) commands the brigade group (Stacey, p. 368; Wikipedia). Opponents: the German garrison of Dunkirk. Context: the date is a representative date (inferred value): the sources give the end of the campaign, not a dated observation on 8 May, so confidence is 0.3.
